kernels.definition: Synovial joints are common movable joints with a joint cavity, articular cartilage, synovial fluid, and supporting ligaments that allow smooth motion.

definitionAnchor.quote: Synovial joints allow for smooth movements between the adjacent bones

facts.text: A key structural feature of a synovial joint is a fluid-filled joint cavity.

anchor.quote: A key structural characteristic for a synovial joint that is not seen at fibrous or cartilaginous joints is the presence of a joint cavity

facts.text: Ligaments support synovial joints by holding bones together and resisting abnormal motion.

anchor.quote: Ligaments support the joint by holding the bones together and resisting excess or abnormal joint motions

kernels.definition: Muscle tissue includes skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle; all are excitable, and contractility lets muscle pull on attachment points and shorten with force.

definitionAnchor.quote: the body contains three types of muscle tissue: skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, and smooth muscle

facts.text: All three muscle tissue types share excitability.

anchor.quote: they all exhibit a quality called excitability

facts.text: Skeletal muscle depends on nervous-system signaling to work properly.

anchor.quote: skeletal muscle completely depends on signaling from the nervous system to work properly

kernels.definition: Nervous tissue is excitable tissue made mainly of neurons and neuroglia; neurons propagate information through electrochemical impulses called action potentials.

definitionAnchor.quote: Two main classes of cells make up nervous tissue: the neuron and neuroglia

facts.text: Nervous tissue sends and receives electrochemical signals that provide the body with information.

anchor.quote: capable of sending and receiving electrochemical signals that provide the body with information

facts.text: Neuroglia support neurons and modulate information propagation.

anchor.quote: Neuroglia play an essential role in supporting neurons and modulating their information propagation

kernels.definition: Sensory receptors detect internal or external stimuli and convert them into nervous-system signals; perception is the central processing of those signals into meaningful patterns.

definitionAnchor.quote: Perception is the central processing of sensory stimuli into a meaningful pattern

facts.text: Receptors are cells or structures that detect sensations.

anchor.quote: Receptors are the cells or structures that detect sensations

facts.text: Stimuli are changed into electrochemical signals of the nervous system.

anchor.quote: Stimuli from varying sources, and of different types, are received and changed into the electrochemical signals of the nervous system

kernels.definition: Hormones circulate through the bloodstream but affect only target cells with the appropriate receptors, triggering target-cell responses that regulate physiological processes.

definitionAnchor.quote: it will affect the activity only of its target cells; that is, cells with receptors for that particular hormone

facts.text: Hormone binding initiates a chain of events that leads to a target-cell response.

anchor.quote: Once the hormone binds to the receptor, a chain of events is initiated that leads to the target cell's response

facts.text: Hormones regulate processes including growth, metabolism, fluid balance, electrolyte balance, and sleep.

anchor.quote: metabolism, fluid, and electrolyte balance, sleep, and many other body functions

mcItems.q: A student examines a joint that moves smoothly because it has a cavity filled with fluid, cartilage on the bone ends, and supporting bands. Which feature most directly identifies the joint as synovial?
op: A fluid-filled joint cavity
Articular cartilage on the bone ends
Supporting bands around the joint
Smooth movement during use
mcItems.ex: A fluid-filled joint cavity is the decisive feature that identifies a synovial joint. The other choices can fit nearby ideas about joint support or movement, but smooth motion is an outcome and the other structures are supporting parts rather than the defining cavity.

mcItems.q: During a lab case, a joint is tested for restraint against an unusual pull so the bones stay aligned while movement remains possible. Which role best matches the structures that provide that restraint?
op: They hold the bones together and resist abnormal motion
They create the joint cavity and its fluid
They cover bone ends with articular cartilage
They produce movement directly by contracting
mcItems.ex: Ligaments hold bones together and resist abnormal motion, which is the decisive supporting role. A common misconception is to treat the smooth movement of the joint as the ligament's job, but movement comes from the joint system overall rather than from ligaments producing force.

keyTerms.df: A common movable joint built around a fluid-filled cavity with cartilage, synovial fluid, and supportive ligaments.
keyTerms.eg: In the case studio, the knee is used as the example of a synovial joint because it can move smoothly while being stabilized by ligaments.
keyTerms.mi: It is just any place where two bones meet, even if there is no cavity.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that a synovial joint is identified by its cavity and related supporting features, not simply by the fact that bones meet.

keyTerms.df: A band of connective tissue that joins bones and helps limit harmful extra motion.
keyTerms.eg: When the course case describes a joint being held together during a sudden sideways force, the ligament is the structure doing that restraint.
keyTerms.mi: It is a muscle that shortens to pull bones through a movement.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that ligaments stabilize the joint; muscles generate force, but ligaments are not contractile tissues.

mcItems.q: A lab case compares three muscle samples. Which sample must rely on nervous-system signaling to work properly?
op: The skeletal muscle sample
The cardiac muscle sample
The smooth muscle sample
The excitable muscle sample
mcItems.ex: The skeletal muscle sample is the only one identified as depending on nervous-system signaling to work properly. A common mistake is to assume all muscle works the same way just because all muscle can contract, but the supplied evidence singles out skeletal muscle for this dependence.

mcItems.q: In a review of muscle tissue, which property is shared by skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle?
op: Excitability
Attachment-point pulling
Nervous-system dependence
Force shortening
mcItems.ex: Excitability is shared by skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle. A nearby misconception is to treat the ability to pull on attachment points or shorten with force as the shared trait, but those describe how muscle contracts rather than the one property all three types have in common.

keyTerms.df: A muscle type that must use nervous-system signaling to function properly.
keyTerms.eg: In a movement case, a skeletal muscle sample only responds correctly when the nervous system provides the needed signal.
keyTerms.mi: It is the same as any muscle that contracts without outside input.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that this tissue is the one specifically tied to nervous-system signaling in the supplied material.

keyTerms.df: The ability to respond to a stimulus in a way that starts activity.
keyTerms.eg: A case note may describe skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle as all showing this shared responsiveness.
keyTerms.mi: It means only one muscle type can contract.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that all three muscle tissue types share this property, not just one of them.

mcItems.q: Which description best fits perception in a sensory pathway?
op: Cells that detect a stimulus and convert it into nervous-system signals
The central processing of those signals into meaningful patterns
A physical change in the environment that is detected
A general term for any detected sensation
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is the central processing of sensory signals into meaningful patterns. A common mix-up is to treat perception as the receptor’s detection step, but detection and signal conversion happen before central processing.

mcItems.q: What do sensory receptors do when they encounter a stimulus?
op: They turn the stimulus into electrochemical nervous-system signals
They assemble those signals into a meaningful pattern
They serve as the sensory experience itself
They are only found in one body location
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is that receptors convert a stimulus into electrochemical nervous-system signals. A likely misconception is to confuse this with perception, but pattern-making happens later in central processing.

keyTerms.df: Cells or structures that detect internal or external stimuli and start sensory signaling.
keyTerms.eg: In this course case, a receptor in skin detects a touch stimulus and begins the nervous-system signal pathway.
keyTerms.mi: They are the same thing as the brain’s interpretation of a sensation.
keyTerms.cx: That interpretation comes later; receptors first detect the stimulus and convert it into signal form.

keyTerms.df: Central processing that organizes sensory signals into meaningful patterns.
keyTerms.eg: After a signal reaches the nervous system, perception lets the body interpret it as a recognizable touch or sound.
keyTerms.mi: It is the moment when a receptor first notices the stimulus.
keyTerms.cx: The first notice happens at the receptor; perception is the later processing step.

mcItems.q: A hormone enters the bloodstream after release from a gland. Which outcome best describes where it will act?
op: Only cells with the matching receptor will respond
Every tissue in the body will respond equally
The hormone works only where it was released
The bloodstream itself is the target tissue
mcItems.ex: Only cells with the appropriate receptor respond to a circulating hormone, so the match between hormone and receptor is the decisive feature. A common mistake is to think blood transport means every cell responds, but the supplied mechanism limits action to target cells.

mcItems.q: A student says a hormone was carried in blood, so the target cell response already happened. What is the best correction?
op: Transport in blood is separate from the response; binding to receptors starts the response
Blood transport and target-cell response are the same event
The hormone causes a response before it reaches any cell
Receptors stop a hormone from circulating
mcItems.ex: Transport through the bloodstream does not by itself produce the response; receptor binding starts a chain of events in the target cell. The nearest-neighbor misconception is to treat movement in blood as the response itself, but the response begins after binding.

keyTerms.df: A cell that responds because it has the appropriate receptor for a hormone.
keyTerms.eg: In a class case, a liver cell with the right receptor changes its activity after a hormone arrives in the blood.
keyTerms.mi: Any cell touched by blood will react to the hormone.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that receptor match, not simple exposure to blood, makes a cell a target.

keyTerms.df: A hormone attaching to its matching receptor and starting events inside the target cell.
keyTerms.eg: In a signaling scenario, the hormone docks on the membrane receptor and the cell then changes its behavior.
keyTerms.mi: Binding is just the same as the hormone being present in the bloodstream.
keyTerms.cx: The fix is that binding is the trigger for downstream change, while bloodstream transport is only the delivery step.

mcItems.q: During a lab case, a joint is tested for restraint against an unusual pull so the bones stay aligned while movement remains possible. Which role best matches the structures that provide that restraint?

They produce movement directly by contracting

mcItems.q: A lab case compares three muscle samples. Which sample must rely on nervous-system signaling to work properly?
op: The skeletal muscle sample
The cardiac muscle sample
The smooth muscle sample
The excitable muscle sample
mcItems.ex: The skeletal muscle sample is the only one identified as depending on nervous-system signaling to work properly. A common mistake is to assume all muscle works the same way just because all muscle can contract, but the supplied evidence singles out skeletal muscle for this dependence.

Attachment-point pulling
Nervous-system dependence
Force shortening

mcItems.q: During a case study, a student needs the structure that sends and receives electrochemical signals to provide the body with information. Which choice matches that role?
op: neuroglia
cartilage cells
nervous tissue
skeletal muscle
mcItems.ex: Nervous tissue is the choice because it sends and receives electrochemical signals that provide the body with information. A near miss is neuroglia: they support neurons and modulate signal propagation, but they are not the tissue described as the main signal-sending and signal-receiving system.

mcItems.q: Which description best matches nervous tissue?
op: Excitable tissue mainly made of neurons and neuroglia that carries action potentials
Connective tissue built mainly from collagen fibers that stores minerals
Epithelial tissue formed mainly by tightly packed cells that line surfaces
Muscle tissue made mainly of fibers that shorten to produce force
mcItems.ex: Correct: nervous tissue is mainly neurons and neuroglia that use action potentials. It is not just support cells; neuroglia support neurons.

keyTerms.df: Excitable body tissue built mainly from neurons and neuroglia, with neurons carrying information in action potentials.
keyTerms.eg: In a lab image from the course, a tissue block with neurons and supporting glia is identified as nervous tissue because it is specialized for signal flow.
keyTerms.mi: It is only the same thing as a nerve bundle outside the brain.
keyTerms.cx: That description is too narrow: the course term refers to the tissue type itself, not just a visible nerve cord or bundle in one location.

keyTerms.df: Support cells in nervous tissue that help neurons and adjust how signals move.
keyTerms.eg: When a case asks which cells help keep neuronal signaling organized during a neural pathway activity, the support cells are neuroglia.
keyTerms.mi: They are the cells that generate the main electrochemical impulses.
keyTerms.cx: The impulses are propagated by neurons; neuroglia assist and shape the signaling environment instead.

mcItems.q: Which description best fits perception in a sensory pathway?
op: Cells that detect a stimulus and convert it into nervous-system signals
The central processing of those signals into meaningful patterns
A physical change in the environment that is detected
A general term for any detected sensation
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is the central processing of sensory signals into meaningful patterns. A common mix-up is to treat perception as the receptor’s detection step, but detection and signal conversion happen before central processing.

mcItems.q: What do sensory receptors do when they encounter a stimulus?
op: They turn the stimulus into electrochemical nervous-system signals
They assemble those signals into a meaningful pattern
They serve as the sensory experience itself
They are only found in one body location
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is that receptors convert a stimulus into electrochemical nervous-system signals. A likely misconception is to confuse this with perception, but pattern-making happens later in central processing.

keyTerms.df: Central processing that organizes sensory signals into meaningful patterns.
keyTerms.eg: After a signal reaches the nervous system, perception lets the body interpret it as a recognizable touch or sound.
keyTerms.mi: It is the moment when a receptor first notices the stimulus.
keyTerms.cx: The first notice happens at the receptor; perception is the later processing step.

keyTerms.df: Sensory receptors are cells or structures that detect internal or external stimuli and convert them into nervous-system signals; perception is the central processing of those signals into meaningful patterns.
keyTerms.eg: A touch receptor in the skin detects pressure and sends a nervous-system signal that the brain interprets as a light tap.
keyTerms.mi: Perception occurs as soon as a receptor detects a stimulus.
keyTerms.cx: Detection starts the signaling process, but the brain creates perception by interpreting those signals into meaning.

mcItems.q: A hormone enters the bloodstream after release from a gland. Which outcome best describes where it will act?
op: Only cells with the matching receptor will respond
Every tissue in the body will respond equally
The hormone works only where it was released
The bloodstream itself is the target tissue
mcItems.ex: Only cells with the appropriate receptor respond to a circulating hormone, so the match between hormone and receptor is the decisive feature. A common mistake is to think blood transport means every cell responds, but the supplied mechanism limits action to target cells.

mcItems.q: A student says a hormone was carried in blood, so the target cell response already happened. What is the best correction?
op: Transport in blood is separate from the response; binding to receptors starts the response
Blood transport and target-cell response are the same event
The hormone causes a response before it reaches any cell
Receptors stop a hormone from circulating
mcItems.ex: Transport through the bloodstream does not by itself produce the response; receptor binding starts a chain of events in the target cell. The nearest-neighbor misconception is to treat movement in blood as the response itself, but the response begins after binding.

keyTerms.df: A cell that responds because it has the appropriate receptor for a hormone.
keyTerms.eg: In a class case, a liver cell with the right receptor changes its activity after a hormone arrives in the blood.
keyTerms.mi: Any cell touched by blood will react to the hormone.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that receptor match, not simple exposure to blood, makes a cell a target.

keyTerms.df: A hormone attaching to its matching receptor and starting events inside the target cell.
keyTerms.eg: In a signaling scenario, the hormone docks on the membrane receptor and the cell then changes its behavior.
keyTerms.mi: Binding is just the same as the hormone being present in the bloodstream.
keyTerms.cx: The fix is that binding is the trigger for downstream change, while bloodstream transport is only the delivery step.
